meta.title: Who really said "I never forget a face, but in your case I'll be glad to make an exception"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Groucho Marx, almost certainly — but not in these words. The joke is documented from 1935; this exact phrasing surfaces later, in a 1964 collection.

answer.label: Attributed to Groucho Marx
answer.authorDates: 1890–1977 · American comedian, actor and game-show host
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes Groucho coined this joke and popularised it: citations point to him from November 1936 onward and no rival claimant is strong. What it does not find is a fixed wording — the early versions all run “I’m going to make an exception in your case.” The phrasing quoted here appears later, and Wikiquote ↗ traces it to Leo Rosten’s The Many Worlds of Leo Rosten (1964).

docMeta.dd: The Many Worlds of Leo Rosten

source.excerpt: Groucho Marx, on meeting a prominent actress, said: “I never forget a face – but I’m going to make an exception in your case.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ dates the earliest match to a December 1935 piece by the screenwriter George Oppenheimer, who gave the punchline to a Groucho-like character rather than to Groucho. QI is careful about that citation and so are we: it verified the article in a 1962 reprint, Hello, Hollywood, and states it “has not yet directly verified the presence of this article in ‘The Hollywood Reporter’”. The first citation naming Groucho himself is Sidney Skolsky’s column of 18 November 1936.

QI’s conclusion is explicit, and so is its caveat: it believes “Groucho Marx coined this joke and popularized it”, that there was “no strong rival”, and that “there was no fixed phrasing for the quotation, but the core joke was invariant.”

None of QI’s early citations — 1935, 1936, two in February 1937, Reader’s Digest in May 1941, Bennett Cerf in 1944, Life in 1949 — match the wording on this page. The closest is a May 1941 Hollywood Reporter column that put “in your case I’m glad to make an exception” in the mouth of John Barrymore, not Groucho.

For the exact wording quoted here, Wikiquote ↗ cites Leo Rosten’s The Many Worlds of Leo Rosten (1964). We checked that reference: Google Books ↗ matches the phrase to page 17 of that volume. The book is in snippet view, so we confirmed the match but could not read the surrounding page.
source.excerptNote: The earliest citation naming Groucho, from Sidney Skolsky’s column of 18 November 1936, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. Note the wording differs from the version people quote today.

author.name: Groucho Marx
author.heading: About Groucho Marx
author.bio: Julius Henry “Groucho” Marx was an American comedian, actor, comic vocalist and game-show host who worked in vaudeville, on Broadway, and in film, radio and television. A master of the one-line retort, he is considered one of America’s greatest comedians — and, inevitably, one of its most quoted, which is why lines he never said keep arriving under his name.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The credit here is broadly right, which makes this a subtler case than most on this site. Groucho really is the likeliest author. What is wrong is the confidence: this is quoted as a fixed, documented Groucho line, and it is not one.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ believes Groucho coined and popularised the joke, and found no strong rival claimant. He appears to have used it repeatedly, including on his radio show.

QI states there was “no fixed phrasing”. Its 1935–1949 citations consistently read “I’m going to make an exception in your case”; the version quoted here is documented later, in Leo Rosten’s 1964 collection per Wikiquote ↗.

A May 1941 Hollywood Reporter column gave the line to Barrymore squelching a drunk at a party, and Joey Adams’s From Gags to Riches (1946) credited the comedian Alan Gale. QI records both and still favours Groucho.

The first known appearance is fiction: a screenwriter’s magazine piece in which a Groucho-like character delivers the punchline and credits a Marx Brothers film. QI has not found the line in that film’s script.

misattribution.truthLine: Almost certainly Groucho’s joke — but not a fixed quotation. Quote Investigator ↗ puts it exactly: there was no fixed phrasing, but the core joke was invariant.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is the Groucho insult in its purest form: a compliment for four words, then the trapdoor. The structure matters more than the wording, which is precisely why the wording never settled — it was a stage weapon, redrawn each time it was used.

That makes it a useful test case. A joke that lives in performance leaves a messy paper trail: columnists paraphrase, digests tidy, anthologies smooth. Asking “what were the exact words?” assumes a fixed original that a working comedian never had.
detailsBody: The trail runs through the gossip columns and humour digests of the 1930s and 1940s — Skolsky in 1936, The Literary Digest and the Los Angeles Times in February 1937, Reader’s Digest in May 1941, Bennett Cerf in The Saturday Review in 1944, and Life in 1949 describing Groucho reprising his old zingers on You Bet Your Life.

Each retelling nudges the phrasing. “I’m going to make an exception” becomes “I’ll make an exception”, then “I’m willing to”, then “I’ll be glad to”. No single version is the counterfeit; the joke simply had no canonical text to depart from.
The competing credits fit the same pattern. A good line at a party gets re-pinned to whoever the teller finds funniest, which is how Barrymore acquired it in 1941 and Alan Gale in 1946.
context.pull: A compliment for four words, then the trapdoor.
